note: Written by internal/v2/tmpl TestWriteDialectConformanceFixtures. Regenerate with LEDGER_WRITE_CONFORMANCE=1 go test ./internal/v2/tmpl/ -run TestWriteDialectConformanceFixtures; do not hand-edit. Patterns are plain JSON strings because a human ports the validator from this file; probe inputs and captured text are base64 because they deliberately contain CR, U+2028, U+2029, U+00A0, U+000B and U+FEFF, which is the point of them. `rejected` pins validator parity: the TypeScript validator must reject each pattern with the same reason codes. `accepted` pins ENGINE parity, which is the stronger claim: for each pattern, what Go's RE2 matched and captured on every probe input, which JavaScript must reproduce exactly.

rejected.why: an empty pattern matches everything; never intended
bounded cost
bounded cost
Go \s is [\t\n\f\r ]; JS \s additionally matches \v, U+00A0, U+FEFF and the Unicode space separators
with the i flag JS's word set gains U+017F and U+212A, Go's does not: (?i)\bk vs /\bk/iu on U+212A is false in Go, true in JS
Go accepts \p{Arabic} and rejects \p{Script=Arabic}; JS under u does the exact opposite
\x{...} is a SyntaxError in JS under u; \u{...} does not compile in Go
\A, \z and \Z compile in Go and are a SyntaxError in JS
backreferences are absent from RE2 and unbounded in JS
\a is BEL in Go and a SyntaxError in JS under u; the escape set is a whitelist, so every such escape is caught, not only the named ones
a trailing backslash is not a pattern
JS has no inline flag groups; declare flags on the Extract entry
lookaround is a backtracking construct and RE2 lacks it
one stored spelling only, so ToJS is total and the stored text is what Go runs
(?P=, (?P> and (?# exist in Go or PCRE and not in JS
Go accepts (?P<0a>...); JS under u rejects it. Go rejects (?<a$b>...); JS accepts it
Go accepts duplicate capture names, JS rejects them
structural
Go's . matches \r, U+2028 and U+2029; JS's does not
an unbounded quantifier on a group is the catastrophic-backtracking shape
(a+)+ nesting turns bounded work exponential in a backtracking engine

the POLYNOMIAL backtracking shape: n^k for k unbounded quantifiers that can consume the same characters. MEASURED in Bun 1.3.14: [0-9]+[0-9]+z is 86 ms on 800 characters, [0-9]+[0-9]+[0-9]+[0-9]+z is 88,191 ms on 400, and separating them with a mandatory literal does not help ([^\n]+X[^\n]+Y is 31,680 ms on 8,000). Go's RE2 does not backtrack and is unaffected, so this is a CLIENT-side cost rule, not an engine divergence

the BOUNDED analogue of unbounded_inside_quantified_group, and the hole it left: a group that repeats more than once re-splits its own contents on every repeat, so a variable-length interior is raised to the power of the repeat count. MEASURED in Bun 1.3.14 on a 512-rune subject: (?:[a-z0-9 ]{1,8}){8}z is 2,178 ms and (?:(?:[a-z]{1,4}){4}){4}z is 1,948 ms, while (?:[a-z]{8}){8}z — the SAME bound product of 64, fixed-width interior — is 0.0 ms, which is why no tightening of MaxBoundProduct separates them. '?' and {0,1} are exempt: one repetition multiplies nothing, and ([0-9]{1,4})? is this table's own rewrite for ([0-9]+)?. RE2 does not backtrack, so this is a client-side cost rule

the same explosion reached by CONCATENATION rather than nesting, which no nesting rule can see: three sibling runs nest nothing and quantify no group. MEASURED in Bun 1.3.14: eight sibling [a-z]{1,8} runs took 7,140 ms on a 512-character body, and [0-9]{1,64}[0-9]{1,64}z took 8,711 ms at MaxBodyBytes (2,000,000 digits) — measured there, not extrapolated from a smaller run. The bound is the number of ways one branch can split the same input, which is what MaxBoundProduct (a bound on match LENGTH) does not measure. 1,024 is exactly the widest collapsible pair MaxBoundProduct still permits: {1,a}{1,b} collapses to {2,a+b}, a+b <= 64 maximises a*b at 32*32; the widest pattern the seed set actually ships is 200, and the widest this rule ADMITS still costs 1,858 ms at MaxBodyBytes
bounded match length
Go reads a{,3} as five literal characters; JS under u makes it a SyntaxError
Go rejects []; JS under u reads it as a class that never matches
structural
Go compiles [[:alpha:]] as a POSIX class; JS under u makes it a SyntaxError, and without u it silently means something else
JS's m treats \r, U+2028 and U+2029 as line terminators for ^/$ and Go's does not
a flag list is a set; a repeat is an authoring mistake
the structural scanner is not a parser; Go's own compiler is the backstop
width 1,025: 25 x 41. One more than the row above, and the only difference between them
two branches of 625 sum to 1,250. A mirror that took the MAX across branches would see 625 and accept it
TWO is where a repetition starts multiplying. Width is only 16 here, so the width rule does not fire and this row isolates the nesting one

an UNBOUNDED interior makes its group variable, so BOTH codes are emitted and in this order. The verdict was never in doubt — unbounded_inside_quantified_group alone refuses it — but the code list is the contract, and a Go mutation that dropped the second code survived the entire suite until this row existed

accepted.name: width-exactly-at-the-limit
accepted.why: width 1,024 = MaxRepetitionWidth exactly, and 1,858 ms against 2,000,000 digits in Bun 1.3.14 — the most expensive pattern the dialect admits

accepted.name: width-branches-sum-they-do-not-multiply
accepted.why: two branches of 500. A mirror that MULTIPLIED alternatives would see 250,000 and refuse it

accepted.name: width-an-unbounded-quantifier-counts-one
accepted.why: if + counted as infinity this would be refused, and the DIB merchant anchor with it

accepted.name: nested-repeats-at-most-once
accepted.why: one repetition multiplies nothing. ([0-9]{1,4})? is the dialect's own rewrite for ([0-9]+)?, so a mirror that refused this would make unbounded_inside_quantified_group inexpressible

accepted.name: nested-fixed-width-interior
accepted.why: the SAME bound product of 64 as (?:[a-z0-9 ]{1,8}){8}, and 0.0 ms against the same subject

to_js.why: every group, not only the first
an ESCAPED paren followed by ?P< is not a named group; a string replace would corrupt it
inside a character class it is five literals

canonical.why: Canonical() is key-sorted, total (no omitempty) and escaped exactly as JSON.stringify escapes: Go's encoding/json escapes &, < and > by default, and escapes U+2028/U+2029 even with SetEscapeHTML(false), while JSON.stringify does neither.

corpus.spec: pats = dialectCorpus() in internal/v2/tmpl/conformance_test.go, transliterated in client/src/tmpl/dialect.test.ts. sha256 over, for each pattern in order: pattern + "\x00" + ValidatePattern(pattern, []).codes.join(",") + "\n", as UTF-8.

engine_notes.name: \s on U+000B
engine_notes.note: the vertical tab is ASCII, so this divergence does not need exotic input

engine_notes.name: . on CR
engine_notes.note: (.+) appears in five of the six v1 seed anchors, which is why the bare dot is banned rather than documented

engine_notes.name: \b with i on U+212A
engine_notes.note: JavaScript's word set gains U+017F and U+212A when i and u are both set; Go's never does

engine_notes.name: \p{Arabic}
engine_notes.note: JS spells it \p{Script=Arabic}, which Go in turn rejects; this corpus is Arabic

engine_notes.name: \a
engine_notes.note: not on the spec's ban list; caught because the escape set is a whitelist

engine_notes.name: [[:alpha:]]
engine_notes.note: without the u flag JS reads it as a class of [ : a l p h followed by literals, silently

engine_notes.name: i without u, literal
engine_notes.note: THE reason the u flag is mandatory on the JavaScript side; with iu both say true

engine_notes.name: i without u, \w
engine_notes.note: same cause; with iu both say true

engine_notes.name: ^ and $ without m
engine_notes.note: an AGREEMENT, recorded because Perl and Python disagree with both: neither Go nor JS matches $ before a trailing newline, which is what makes the m flag ban free

engine_notes.name: cost: [0-9]+[0-9]+z
engine_notes.note: two unbounded quantifiers that consume the same characters is O(n^2) in a backtracking engine

engine_notes.name: cost: [0-9]+[0-9]+[0-9]+[0-9]+z
engine_notes.note: 88 SECONDS on a 400-character attacker-chosen input; this is the measurement the rule was written for

engine_notes.name: cost: [^\n]+X[^\n]+Y
engine_notes.note: separating the two quantifiers with a MANDATORY literal does not make the shape cheap, it only changes which input triggers it — which is why the rule counts rather than looking for adjacency

engine_notes.name: cost: [0-9]{1,64}[0-9]+z
engine_notes.note: bounding one of the two is NOT the sanctioned rewrite: the bound becomes the constant. Collapsing them is: [0-9]+[0-9]+ is [0-9]{2,}

engine_notes.name: cost: [0-9]+z (the residual)
engine_notes.note: ONE unbounded quantifier is still quadratic, and the dialect allows it. What keeps the real templates cheap is their leading literal anchor: the DIB merchant anchor on a hostile 1 MB body is 1.9 ms. See TestKNOWNASingleUnboundedQuantifierIsStillQuadraticInJavaScript

engine_notes.name: bun: [a-z] with iu on U+212A
engine_notes.js: true in V8 and WebKit, FALSE in Bun 1.3.14
engine_notes.note: A BUN BUG, not a dialect issue: Go, V8 and WebKit 26.5 all match, so the shipping client (a browser) agrees with the server and no rule is needed. It matters only because `bun test` is this repository's gate, so a conformance probe that relied on case-insensitive folding of a class RANGE into a non-ASCII code point would fail in CI while the real client was correct. client/src/tmpl/agreement.test.ts pins it so a Bun fix is noticed rather than silently changing what the gate means.
